Monday night. I woke up thirsty at five and saw the kitchen light on. My father Imran was standing there in his vest, rolling rotis for my tiffin, yawning so hard his eyes were wet. I never knew he did that. I always thought the tiffin just appeared.
At lunch I opened the box and my roti was shaped like a star with a little tomato heart. Something went warm in my tummy, and I felt a bit bad that I once said "not this sabzi again."
When I got home I said, "Papa, thanks for the star roti. I saw you at five." He looked shy and said, "Eat well, Sahil." Next week I'll wake up and help.
Sahil

qa.q: What was the shape of the roti in Sahil's tiffin?
qa.a: A star with a little tomato heart.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when opening the tiffin box at lunch?
qa.a: Warm inside, and a bit guilty about once complaining about the sabzi.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that turned noticing into thanks?
qa.a: Sahil thanked Papa for the star roti, said Sahil had seen him at five, and planned to wake up and help next week.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when Sahil thanks him?
qa.a: Shy and pleased. He looks shy and tells Sahil to eat well, so the thanks clearly matters even though he does not say much. 🙂

grounding: A child begins to see the effort behind a parent's cooking and says so.

In the village school, Keerthana Madam had shown the class how to add fractions three times, and Zubin still did not get it. He watched her draw the same pie on the board a fourth time, chalk dust on her blue sari, her voice as calm as the first time.
Suddenly he saw it. She could have shouted, and she never did. She had stayed after the bell most days to help slow ones like him, and her sandals were grey with the walk from the next village.
After class he stayed behind. "Madam, thank you for showing us again," he said. "I know you're tired."
She blinked, then smiled. "Come, one more pie." This time it made sense.

qa.q: How many times had Keerthana Madam shown the class how to add fractions before the fourth pie?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Zubin realise about Keerthana as he watched her draw the pie a fourth time?
qa.a: That she could have shouted but stayed calm and patient, and that she gave her time to slow learners, so he felt grateful.

qa.q: What did Zubin do after class that made his gratitude real?
qa.a: He stayed behind and thanked Keerthana Madam for showing them again, saying he knew she was tired.

qa.q: How might Keerthana Madam feel when Zubin thanks her?
qa.a: Surprised and touched. She blinks, smiles and offers one more pie.

grounding: A child begins to see the effort behind a teacher's patience and says so.

You want to know why I stopped talking at dinner, Santosh? Okay. I'm Gautam. I once said the maths tuition was too much, and my mother said, "Do you know there are children who don't have a school to go to? Be grateful." And she kept going. Every complaint got answered with somebody who had less.
I sat there feeling like garbage, guilty for being tired, and honestly angry too, because my day was still my day. I stopped complaining. That didn't make me grateful. It made me quiet.
Last month my aunt said, "It's a lot, isn't it? And you also have some lucky things." Both could be true. That was the first time I actually felt thankful, and I told her so.

qa.q: What did Gautam's mother say when Gautam said the tuition was too much?
qa.a: She said there are children who don't have a school to go to, and told Gautam to be grateful.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel while being told to be grateful?
qa.a: Guilty for being tired and angry too, because the day still felt real. Gautam felt like garbage.

qa.q: What did the aunt say that changed things for Gautam?
qa.a: She said it is a lot and that Gautam also has some lucky things, letting both be true, and then Gautam felt thankful and said so.

qa.q: How might Gautam's mother see her own words?
qa.a: She may think she is teaching thankfulness, without noticing that each complaint is answered with someone who has less, which shuts Gautam down.

grounding: A teenager told to be grateful by comparison with poorer children feels guilt and resentment and stops speaking honestly.

I'm Mehak, and I sit behind Dolma in class. Last Tuesday Dolma was close to tears over a low mark, and our teacher said, "Some children would give anything to be in this school. Be grateful." Dolma went quiet and sat very straight.
At lunch she pushed her food around and said, "Now I feel bad for being sad." I don't know exactly what was in her head, but I noticed she stopped telling anyone when she was upset.
Later I sat next to her and said, "You can be sad about the mark and still be glad to be here." Her shoulders came down a little. I think she just needed both to be allowed.

qa.q: What did the teacher say to Dolma about the low mark?
qa.a: That some children would give anything to be in this school, and to be grateful.

qa.a: Mehak said Dolma can be sad about the mark and still be glad to be here. That let both feelings be allowed, so Dolma's shoulders came down.

qa.q: What might the teacher have hoped for by saying it?
qa.a: Probably to give perspective or comfort, but it shut Dolma's feelings down instead.

Sabina here. Raghav sits opposite me, and for months I noticed a small ritual: at half past five, before shutting down, he wrote three lines in a tiny blue notebook. I asked once. "Three good things from today," he said. "But specific. Not 'family' or 'health,' those bore me. Today: the cook put extra jaggery in my tea without asking, a client said 'that was clear,' and the pigeon on the sill finally left."
I laughed. But over the months he seemed to notice more and complain less at lunch. I can't say it's all the notebook. He also started pointing out good things to me, too. Yesterday it was "the printer worked first time." We celebrated with biscuits.

qa.q: What did Raghav write in the tiny blue notebook at half past five?
qa.a: Three good things from the day.

qa.q: What might Raghav be feeling at half past five when he writes his three lines?
qa.a: Content and attentive. Small, specific things like extra jaggery or a client's compliment seem to give him quiet pleasure.

qa.q: What makes Raghav's list work better than a general one?
qa.a: He writes specific, fresh items and avoids generic words like family or health, so he has to notice real moments.

qa.q: What does Sabina think the notebook has done for Raghav?
qa.a: Sabina thinks Raghav notices more and complains less, though Sabina cannot say it is all the notebook.

grounding: A young adult writes three specific good things at the end of the day and their attention shifts toward what works.

Day 1. Darshan wrote his first gratitude list: family, health, job. It felt like filling in a form, and he closed the notebook without feeling anything.
Day 6. His flatmate Manjula looked at the list. "Too generic," she said. "What made you smile today?" He thought. That evening he wrote: The fruit seller kept the ripe mango aside for me. My bus came just as I reached the stop. Manjula's terrible joke about the geyser.
Day 20. Walking to work, Darshan caught himself noticing the steam from the chai stall and a neighbour's rangoli, so he would have something to write. His shoulders had dropped without his noticing.

qa.a: Family, health, job.

qa.q: What did Darshan feel about his first list?

passage:
Sunday. Kunal was clearing an old shelf when he found his Class 10 physics notebook and, on the last page, a blue-inked note: "Kunal, you can do this. Vasudha Ma'am." He remembered the evening she stayed an extra hour to explain motion, when he was ready to quit science.
Tuesday. He wrote her a message and deleted it twice. The third version said: "Ma'am, you stayed late to teach me motion when I wanted to give up. I'm an engineer now, and I still use that page. Thank you." He sent it before he could stop himself.
Friday. Her reply: "I remember you. I read this three times at lunch. It made my week."

qa.q: What did Kunal find on the last page of his physics notebook?
qa.a: A blue-inked note: 'Kunal, you can do this. Vasudha Ma'am.'

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he wrote and deleted the message twice?
qa.a: Nervous and shy, but grateful enough to send it before he could stop himself.

qa.q: What made Kunal's thank-you specific and strong?
qa.a: He named what she did, staying late to teach him motion, what it meant, that he wanted to quit, and what came of it, that he is an engineer now.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel on receiving the message?
qa.a: Touched and happy. She says she remembers Kunal, read the message three times and that it made her week.

grounding: A person sends a specific thank-you to a teacher, naming what she did and how it mattered.

passage:
Raghav, listen. Forty years ago your grandfather Harish nearly failed his apprenticeship. There was an old fitter at the railway workshop, Bapu Iyer, who showed me how to read a gauge when nobody else had time. I never thanked him. I thought a good worker's thanks was the work.
Years later I met him at a station, stooped and half deaf, and I said, "Bapu, you taught me the gauge. Because of that I've fed my family." He gripped my hand and wept. Then he laughed and said, "Nobody ever told me."
I was ashamed it had taken twenty years. Don't wait for the perfect moment. Tell them what they gave you and what it changed.

qa.q: What was the old fitter's name?
qa.a: Bapu Iyer.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when he realised how long he had waited to thank Bapu Iyer?
qa.a: Ashamed that it had taken twenty years.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make at the station that changed things?
qa.a: Harish told Bapu Iyer straight out that Bapu had taught the gauge and that Harish's family was fed because of it.

qa.q: How did Bapu Iyer react to being thanked?
qa.a: He gripped Harish's hand and wept, then laughed and said nobody had ever told him.

grounding: An elder recalls finally thanking a mentor directly and naming what he did and how it mattered.

At the playground in Lisbon, Nour stood at the top of the little slide, toes over the edge. She looked down, then back at her father Tomas, standing at the bottom with open arms. She hugged the rail and whimpered.
"Take your time," said Tomas.
Nour lifted a foot, put it down, lifted it again. Then, with a tiny squeal, she sat, pushed, and whooshed into his arms. She stared up, astonished, and shouted, "Again!"

qa.q: Where did Nour hesitate?
qa.a: At the top of the little slide.

qa.q: What is Nour feeling at the top of the slide?
qa.a: Scared but wanting to try. She hugs the rail, whimpers and lifts a foot, then puts it down.

qa.q: What did Tomas do that helped Nour?
qa.a: He stood at the bottom with open arms and said 'Take your time', without pushing.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel when Nour shouts 'Again!'?
qa.a: Delighted and relieved, since he waited patiently and caught her.

grounding: A toddler hesitates at the top of a slide, glances at a parent, then goes.

Guests were due in ten minutes, and his father Sahil was rushing about with a tray. Omkar reached for the blue cup. It slipped and cracked on the floor. He froze, hands behind his back.
Papa's back was turned. Omkar's tummy felt tight, but he tiptoed over and said, in a very small voice, "Papa, I broke the blue cup."
Sahil stopped. He looked at the pieces, then at Omkar's face. "Thank you for telling me. Stay back, I'll sweep, and you can hold the dustpan."
Omkar let out a huge breath and held the dustpan very still.

qa.q: How many minutes until the guests arrived?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling after the cup cracked?
qa.a: Frightened. He froze with his hands behind his back and his tummy felt tight.

qa.q: What did Omkar choose to do next, and what happened?
qa.a: Omkar tiptoed over and told Papa, and Sahil thanked him and gave him a job holding the dustpan.

qa.q: How might Sahil's reaction affect the next time Omkar breaks something?
qa.a: Because Sahil stayed calm and thanked him, honesty will feel safe, so Omkar is more likely to tell again.

grounding: A child owns up to a broken cup despite fear of a scolding, and a calm adult response makes honesty feel safe.

Dolma was carrying Dada's tea cup to the balcony when it slipped. Crash.
Dada Vijay came running. "Careful! That was my favourite cup!" he said sharply.
Dolma's lip wobbled and her eyes filled, but she stayed put. "I dropped it," she whispered. "I'm sorry."
Vijay's face changed. He knelt slowly and cleared his throat. "That came out too loud. Thank you for telling me straight away. It's only a cup, and you're not hurt, are you?"
She shook her head. Together they picked up the big pieces.

qa.q: What did Dolma drop?
qa.a: Dada's tea cup.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Vijay spoke sharply?
qa.a: Scared and upset. Her lip wobbled and her eyes filled, but she stayed and owned up.

qa.q: What did Vijay do to repair the moment?
qa.a: He knelt, said his voice had been too loud, thanked her for telling him at once and helped pick up the pieces.

qa.q: How might Vijay's change of tone shape Dolma's next mistake?
qa.a: Dolma will more likely admit it, since honesty got thanks after the sharp first words.

grounding: A child admits to a broken cup though she fears scolding, and the adult's reaction decides whether honesty feels safe.

The school bus was loud and packed, and a group at the back had started copying the way Jahnavi stumbles over her words. Everyone laughed. Kashish felt her heart pounding in her throat; she was afraid of being the next joke. Jahnavi stared out of the window, her ears red.
The bus would reach the school gate in three minutes. Kashish stood up, gripping the seat, and said, "Stop it. That's mean." Her voice shook. Two of them rolled their eyes, but the laughing stopped.
At school Kashish told the class teacher what had happened. The teacher thanked her, sat with Jahnavi at break, and said the head would hear about it that afternoon.

At lunch break, three boys held their noses at Yash's tiffin and made loud sniffing noises. Yash's face crumpled.
Ayesha's heart thumped so hard she could feel it in her ears. She didn't want to be laughed at either. But she put down her spoon and said, "It smells good. Leave him alone."
The table went quiet. Then someone said, "Now she's the teacher's pet." Her cheeks burned. The group moved to another bench, taking her usual seat with them.
Ayesha sat down with her tiffin beside Yash, feeling smaller than before but oddly steady.
The next day Yash slid over and offered her half a paratha.

qa.q: What did speaking up cost Ayesha, and what did she gain?

In the corridor after games, Bhupen watched two older boys shove his friend Nikhil against the lockers and take his cap. He wanted to shout, but his mouth would not move. He stood there until they left.
By afternoon the story had spread, and a classmate hissed, "You just stood there. Coward." Bhupen's ears burned and he could not eat.
At the end of the day Devika Ma'am found him sitting alone. "Tell me," she said. He did, in pieces. "Freezing isn't cowardice," she said. "This is not your fault. And telling me now takes courage."
She walked with him to the counsellor's office, then went to find Nikhil, and the head was told before the bell. At the next break Bhupen went and sat beside Nikhil.

qa.q: Who did the older boys shove against the lockers?
qa.a: Bhupen's friend Nikhil.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel when a classmate called him a coward?
qa.a: Ashamed and miserable. His ears burned and he could not eat.

qa.q: What did Devika Ma'am do that day?
qa.a: She listened, told Bhupen that freezing is not cowardice and not his fault, took him to the counsellor, found Nikhil and made sure the head was told before the bell.

qa.q: How might Nikhil feel when Bhupen sits beside him at break?
qa.a: Probably relieved and supported, since someone stays close after what happened.

grounding: A child who froze when a friend was bullied is called a coward and feels ashamed; a teacher responds the same day.

I'm Kamal, and I saw it at the bus stop. A boy from our school was being jeered at by older kids, and Vikas, who is in my class, stood beside me and didn't say a word. Later someone called him a coward in the class group chat. Vikas read it, went white, and didn't come to cricket. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he looked ashamed.
On Monday I walked with him to the class teacher and we told them about the older kids and the messages. The teacher listened, said freezing isn't cowardice, and that same day spoke to the boy who had been jeered, called his parents and told the older kids' house teacher. They told Vikas that speaking up now was brave.

qa.q: Where did Kamal see the older kids jeering at the boy?

Tushar's diary, Saturday evening. On the school trip today Sumit climbed over the railing of the old canal bridge for a dare. Half the group were filming and shouting his name. He was smiling for the phones, not looking down. My stomach dropped. I shouted, and two of the older boys hauled him back over.
I sent the group to the bus, sat Sumit down with water, checked he was unhurt and rang his mother right there. Later I asked what it was for. "Everyone said I wouldn't," he said.
I thought of the bird-rescue day last year, when he waded in to free a trapped kite and nobody was watching. I wonder which Sumit is the braver one. Monday: speak to the head and the group.

qa.a: On the old canal bridge.

qa.a: Tushar shouted, had older boys haul Sumit back, sent the group to the bus, checked Sumit was unhurt and rang Sumit's mother at once.

qa.q: How does Sumit explain the climb?
qa.a: Sumit says everyone said he wouldn't, so the dare served an audience, unlike the kite rescue, which nobody watched.

passage:
My name is Lokesh. My first venture was a small tiffin delivery business, and it closed after eight months, with debts. I hid at home for weeks. Then Vishal, my old manager, asked me out for coffee and said, "What did you learn?" I said everything I did was too big, too fast.
So I tried again. This time it was one lane of the city, ten customers, no loan, and a page for every rupee. My hands still shook when I knocked on the first door. It didn't feel like courage. It felt like taking one step and checking my footing.
That was a year ago. Now there are ninety customers, and I sleep at night.

qa.q: How many customers did Lokesh start with the second time?
qa.a: Ten customers in one lane of the city.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when knocking on the first door?
qa.a: Shaky and frightened. It did not feel like courage but like taking one step and checking the footing.

qa.q: What did Lokesh change in the second attempt?
qa.a: Lokesh started smaller, with one lane, ten customers and no loan, and kept a page for every rupee.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Lokesh's failure?
qa.a: Vishal treats it as something to learn from, asking 'What did you learn?' over coffee rather than judging.

grounding: After a failed venture, a person tries again with less illusion and more preparation, in small doable steps.
